questions.question: Which design can best support a cause-and-effect conclusion?
questions.explanation: Random assignment makes the groups alike on average in every respect, so a difference in outcome can be attributed to the treatment.

questions.question: In a study of coffee and heart disease, smokers drink more coffee and also have more heart disease. Smoking is a...
questions.explanation: A confounder is linked to both the exposure and the outcome and can create or hide an association.

questions.question: Why does random assignment help?
options: It balances known and unknown factors between the groups, on average
questions.explanation: Randomisation spreads all characteristics, measured or not, evenly across groups on average, so the treatment is the only systematic difference.

questions.question: Treatment A beats B within small stones and within large stones, but B looks better overall. What is this called?
questions.explanation: A trend in every subgroup that reverses when the groups are combined is Simpson's paradox, here caused by stone size (a confounder).

questions.question: In a self-selected study the treatment looks harmful even though it truly helps. If you triple the sample size, what happens to the estimate?
options: It moves to the true value
It stays biased, just more precisely
It becomes significant in the other direction
questions.explanation: A larger sample shrinks random error, not bias. The estimate settles on the wrong value with greater confidence.

questions.question: A double-blind trial means...
options: The sample is twice as large
Neither participants nor those measuring the outcome know who got which treatment
Both groups get the real treatment
questions.explanation: Hiding assignments from both patients and assessors prevents expectations from influencing behaviour or measurements.

questions.question: With σ = 10 and a smallest important difference of 5, about how many people per group give 80% power at α = 0.05?
A magazine studies only the companies that are still successful after 20 years and concludes that bold risk-taking leads to success. Which bias is this?
questions.explanation: Companies that took bold risks and failed have vanished from the sample. Looking only at survivors gives a skewed picture.
